cases.title: Wind tunnel: flow past a sphere
cases.question: At the Reynolds numbers the tunnel resolves, does it reproduce measured sphere drag?
cases.reference: Standard drag curve, Clift & Gauvin (1971), fitted to sphere measurements
cases.note: 16 cells per diameter, laminar (no sub-grid model), 8 × 8 diameter cross-section (1.2 % blockage).

rows.label: Sphere lift at Re 100 (symmetry: should be 0)
Sphere lift at Re 300 (symmetry: should be 0)

findings: Sphere drag within 5 % of the standard curve at its own Reynolds number: the solver, boundary conditions and force measurement are sound. The remaining excess comes mainly from the staircase surface of a 16-cell sphere.

cases.title: Wind tunnel: Ahmed body
cases.question: For a car-like body, does the tunnel reproduce measured drag and its dependence on rear slant?
cases.reference: Ahmed, Ramm & Faltin (1984), SAE 840300, at Re 4.3·10⁶
cases.note: Simulated at Re 5·10³ with 64 cells along the body; stilts omitted; moving road.
findings: Absolute drag is +217 % to +274 % off: at a lattice Reynolds number of 5·10³ the boundary layers are laminar and far too thick, so friction and wake drag dominate. Real cars run at 10⁶-10⁷.
The slant-angle trend (drag peaks near 25-30°, then drops once the flow fully separates) is not reproduced: the separation physics behind it needs turbulent, wall-resolved flow.
Use the tunnel to see flow structure and to compare large shape changes; take absolute Cd from a wind tunnel or coast-down test and enter it as measured.
